newsitem.title: GERMANY: Low rates show no inflation expectations-Tietmeyer.
newsitem.headline: Low rates show no inflation expectations-Tietmeyer.

text.p: Hans Tietmeyer, head of Germany's Bundesbank, was quoted on Friday as saying that low capital market yields showed there were no expectations that price pressures would gather pace.

Asked in a newspaper interview why low German interest rates were failing to stimulate investment, Tietmeyer said: "Capital market interest rates are at the lowest ever. That shows there are no inflation expectations here at the moment."
Low rates show no inflation expectations-Tietmeyer
Tietmeyer added that weak investment was due to the tangle of regulations hindering enterprise in Germany: "It is very difficult to carry out new investment. We must change our way of thinking."

In the interview, to be published on Saturday in the south German Schwarzwaelder Bote newspaper, Tietmeyer also said European monetary union (EMU) would yield economic benefits only if the planned euro currency is stable.
"If the euro comes and it is stable, then it brings significant economic advantages," he told the newspaper.

"But it would be problematic if the euro is introduced and then there are conflicts between the participating countries -- for example if a weak euro created tensions or some countries could not keep up with the stability policies," he added.
Creating the right basis for EMU was important, because a later failure of the currency union could create "a big problem".

Tietmeyer, along with German Finance Minister Theo Waigel, has been an ardent advocate of a strict interpretation of EMU's guiding Maastricht treaty -- particularly of its budget deficit target of three percent of gross domestic product.
Countries must be judged to have met the Maastricht criteria this year to take part in the launch of the single currency planned in 1999.

He said any efforts to alter or embellish budget figures should be opposed, because countries needed to cut back on borrowing regardless of EMU. "We need to save, whether we go ahead with the euro or not," Tietmeyer said.
